findings.fault: The page's one action links to '#', not to a mailto: address. A visitor who clicks the white email button gets nothing. Showing the address was the brief's fix, but the link behind it still has to work.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer ready to write to Mark clicks the only action on the page and nothing happens. They have to copy the address by hand or give up.

findings.where: First screen, the five topic pills (PPP Law, Infrastructure, Development banks, Governments, Risk allocation), p10–p14
findings.fault: These are static labels drawn as outlined capsules with their own boxes, which is how filter chips or buttons look. Nothing happens when they are clicked. They also sit right above the boxed email action, so the page shows two sets of control-like shapes and only one of them works.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who wants Mark's PPP Law work clicks 'PPP Law' to filter or open it and nothing happens. That is a false affordance on the first screen.

findings.where: First screen, the blue field's diagonal stripe pattern, against the Texture specimen card ('No texture: one flat field, no grain and no gradient') and the motion-sketch preview, which is flat
findings.fault: Fine diagonal hatching covers the hero field, under the heading, the lead and the photo. The tile's own Texture card and motion preview describe and show a flat field. The hatching makes the ground busier than the 'one soft ground' the brief asks for, gives it a drafting-sheet, techy feel, and means the specimen misdescribes the page.
findings.who_objects: The founder judges the first screen against the tile's stated rules and gets a ground the tile says is not there. Mark asked for nothing 'in-your-face techy' and finds busy grounds off-putting (brand sheet §6).

findings.where: Article specimen: the caption under the TV-studio photo, the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?', the three-item list and the 'Streamlining the PPP Process' row (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The text rhythm breaks exactly where the brief said it must hold. The subhead sits almost against the caption with no space above it. The list is set solid, much tighter than the body text's line spacing, so wrapped items on phone run into one another. The hairline and the lecture link sit right under the last list line, so the PDF row reads as part of the list rather than a separate item.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Angélique, who were promised a rhythm that survives her adding an image, caption, list and subhead. Readers also lose track of where the article ends and the publication list begins.

findings.where: Article specimen: the list bullets and the 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' link, against the palette ('Four colours and no accent'; links in house blue) and 'Play again' in blue
findings.fault: An orange-red that is not in the palette colours the bullets and the article link. One page now has two link colours, blue for 'Play again' and orange-red here. It is also a hue outside the house blue and grey that the brief binds every tile to.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for the house colours as the only ink. A reader also cannot learn one link colour when the page uses two.

findings.where: First screen, the oversized ghost 'PPP' letters behind the heading; on phone, a cropped 'PP' fragment off the right edge
findings.fault: A second decorative element sits under the one large line and blurs its letterforms. On phone it is cut off and reads as a rendering artefact. The research asked for scale contrast, not more elements.
findings.who_objects: Visitors reading the heading through the shapes behind it. The founder, who asked for refined, not decorative.

findings.where: Phone, first screen order: nav, then the full-width portrait, then the heading, then the email action
findings.fault: On phone the portrait takes the whole first screen. Mark's line starts at the bottom of it and the email action is about two screens down, so the first screen has no message and no action.
findings.who_objects: An officer who opens the link from LinkedIn on a phone sees a headshot and a nav bar. They do not see what Mark says or how to reach him without scrolling.

findings.where: Article specimen: the article title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' and the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?'
findings.fault: The subhead is set at nearly the same size and weight as the article title, so the title does not clearly outrank its own section heading.
findings.who_objects: A reader scanning the article cannot tell the page title from a section break.

findings.fault: Nothing above the fold proves his work: no named body, place or date. The tags are subject labels, not evidence. The visitor has to take the lead sentence on trust.
findings.who_objects: A procurement-minded bank officer, who judges an advisor by work for bodies like theirs (first-visit trust, items 3 and 13).

findings.fault: The mark comes first and Mark's name sits after it in a modest size, little bigger than the descriptor line under it. The brief asks for his name to lead with the logo beside it.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose personal-advisor test puts Mark's name ahead of the firm's mark.

findings.where: Specimen block, desktop: the Type pair row and the Texture column
findings.fault: The 'Source Sans 3' specimen sits about 80 px lower than the Gelasio specimen beside it, and a large empty area is left under the Texture card. The two-column specimen looks unaligned.
findings.who_objects: The founder reading the tile, for whom the misalignment undercuts the 'placed, calm, exact' claim.
